title: Reporting with TRIPOD+AI
text:
TRIPOD+AI (Collins et al. 2024) is the reporting guideline for studies that develop or validate a clinical prediction model, whether by regression or machine learning. The table maps the methods and results topics of its checklist that depend on the analysis to the clinpred output that documents them. Items on the study design, data sources, ethics, and open science are outside any software.








TRIPOD+AI topic
What to report
Where in clinpred




Sample size
how the sample size was decided; whether it was adequate
Sample size adequacy table (criteria of Riley et al.)


Missing data
how missing data were handled
Missing values: exploration and patterns tables; the method note under Data


Data preparation
coding of predictors, transformations
effects table (reference levels, scaling); Model equation (spline knots, coding)


Type of model, building
model type, predictor selection, interactions
selection and interaction tables, with their notes (method, criterion, baseline covariates)


Internal validation
method, and that it includes all modelling steps
performance note (bootstrap or cross-validation; selection repeated in each fit)


Performance measures
discrimination, calibration, clinical utility
Performance tables; calibration plot; decision curve


Updating
methods to update the model in validation data
Model updating table and note


Heterogeneity / fairness
performance across subgroups or settings
performance per validation set; case-mix table


Participants
numbers, outcome events
Data table (per data set, with excluded rows)


Characteristics
predictors by outcome; development vs validation
Descriptives; case-mix table


Full model
all coefficients, intercept, baseline risk
Model coefficients; Model equation; Export model (JSON)


Performance
with confidence intervals; optimism corrected
Performance in the Development Data (apparent, CI, corrected); Performance in the Validation Data


Calibration
calibration plot and measures
calibration plot; calibration-in-the-large, slope, O/E, ICI


Updating results
the updated model and its performance
Model updating table



Two habits help a report:

Report the corrected numbers, not the apparent ones, for the development data, and say how many bootstrap samples (or folds and repeats) were used — the note under the performance table has it.
Give the model: the equation with the spline formula and the baseline survival at the horizon, or the exported JSON as a supplement. A model that cannot be computed by a reader cannot be validated by anyone else.





 Back to topReferences

Collins, Gary S, Karel G M Moons, Paula Dhiman, et al. 2024. “TRIPOD+AI Statement: Updated Guidance for Reporting Clinical Prediction Models That Use Regression or Machine Learning Methods.” BMJ 385 (April): e078378. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-078378.

title: Validation and updating
text:
The previous page defined the measures; this one is about which patients they are measured in. A model measured in the patients it was fitted to looks better than it is (apparent performance, see overfitting). The designs differ in how they find patients the model has not seen. In the figure, each square is a patient of a small development data set of 12.





















Figure 1: Five designs on a data set of 12 patients (numbers are patient identifiers). Blue: the patients the model is fitted on; orange: the patients its performance is measured in. Each bootstrap model is also tested in its own sample, to measure its optimism.




Apparent: fit and test on the same 12 patients. Optimistic: the model has already seen the answers.
Split sample: fit on 8, test on the other 4. Honest but wasteful — the model is built on two thirds of the data and tested on a handful — and the result depends on which patients happened to land in the test part. Not recommended (Steyerberg 2019).
Cross-validation: split into k folds (here 4); fit on 3 folds and predict the fourth, four times, so that every patient is predicted exactly once by a model that did not see them. Repeating with new random splits (repeated cross-validation) averages out the luck of the split.
Bootstrap: draw 12 patients with replacement from the 12 — some appear twice or three times, others not at all (sample 1 misses patients 1, 7, 9). Fit on the bootstrap sample, and measure the performance twice: in the bootstrap sample (where it is optimistic, as apparent performance is) and in the original 12. The difference is the optimism of that model. Repeated 200 times and averaged, it estimates how optimistic the real model is; subtracting it from the apparent performance gives the optimism-corrected performance (HARRELL et al. 1996).
External: the model, fitted on all development patients, is applied unchanged to patients from another hospital or a later period (N1–N8), who played no part in building it.

Cross-validation and the bootstrap are internal validation: they estimate performance in new patients from the same population. Only external validation tests whether the model works elsewhere.







flowchart LR
  A["Development data<br/>(n patients)"] --> B["Fit the model<br/>apparent performance"]
  A --> C["Draw a bootstrap sample<br/>(n patients, with replacement)"]
  C --> D["Repeat the whole procedure<br/>(selection, tuning, fit)"]
  D --> E["Performance in the<br/>bootstrap sample"]
  D --> F["Performance in the<br/>original data"]
  E --> G["Optimism = E − F"]
  F --> G
  G --> H["Average over 200 samples<br/>corrected = apparent − optimism"]
  B --> H






The key is the box Repeat the whole procedure: everything that was done to build the model — variable selection, choice of interactions, the elastic net’s λ — is repeated in every bootstrap sample, so its optimism is included. clinpred does this automatically: the fitting procedure is a single function, used for the final model and for every resampled fit (and for every fold of cross-validation).
Two by-products come free:

the uniform shrinkage factor, the mean calibration slope of the bootstrap models in the original data (how much the coefficients should be shrunk), next to van Houwelingen’s heuristic estimate;
prediction stability (Riley and Collins 2023): each bootstrap model predicts every patient, so the spread of a patient’s predicted risk across models (the instability plot, the mean absolute prediction error, MAPE) shows how much an individual prediction depends on the particular data.

The bootstrap is preferred for small and moderate data sets (it uses all patients to fit); repeated cross-validation behaves similarly when data are large. clinpred stratifies the folds by the outcome.

title: Validation and updating
text:
External validation and case-mix
clinpred applies the development model, unchanged (the same coefficients and, for Cox models, the same baseline hazard), to

the rows marked by a validation split variable in the same data set (a later recruitment period — temporal validation; another centre — geographical), and/or
an external data file (csv, tsv, txt, omv, xlsx, sav). Its columns are matched by name (ignoring case), its factor levels to the development levels, and a check table reports what could not be matched or lies beyond the development range.

Whether performance holds or drops must be interpreted against the case-mix of the new population (Debray et al. 2015). clinpred’s case-mix table compares the predictors, the spread of the linear predictor (a wider spread raises discrimination by itself) and a membership c-statistic: how well a model can tell development from validation patients. Near 0.5 the validation tests reproducibility (same kind of patients); high values test transportability to a different population. For Cox models see also Royston and Altman (2013).

title: Validation and updating
section: Updating a model that does not transport
text:
Updating a model that does not transport
A model rarely fails completely in a new population. More often it still ranks patients well but its risks are off: the new population has a different baseline risk (another country, period or referral pattern), or the predictors carry less weight there. The model does not need to be rebuilt: it can be updated with a few parameters estimated in the new data (Steyerberg 2019; Houwelingen 2000). Writing LP for the original model’s linear predictor (its log-odds), the methods are:









Method
Updated model
Re-estimated
Parameters




Original model
logit(risk) = LP

Recalibration in the large
logit(risk) = a + LP
the intercept: the overall risk level

Recalibration
logit(risk) = a + b × LP

Model revision
every coefficient refitted

For Cox models, a re-estimates the baseline risk at the horizon instead of an intercept.
The figure shows a simulated example: a model developed in one population, validated in another with a higher event rate and weaker effects.





















Figure 2: Calibration in the new population. Left: the original model’s curve is flatter than the diagonal — its predictions are too extreme, low risks too low and high risks too high — and lies above it for most patients (more events than predicted overall). Middle: a new intercept fixes the average level but not the spread. Right: a new intercept and slope fix both.




Original: O/E = 1.44 — 44% more events than predicted — and a calibration slope of 0.52.
Recalibration in the large shifts every log-odds by a = 0.53: the average risk is now right (O/E = 1.00), but low risks are still too low and high risks too high.
Recalibration also multiplies the log-odds by b = 0.52, shrinking them toward the average: the curve now follows the diagonal.

Updating changes the risks, not the ranking: the AUC is the same for the first three methods, because adding a constant or multiplying by a positive number does not reorder patients. Only revision, which re-weights the predictors, can change it.

Choosing the method: the closed testing procedure
More parameters always fit the new data better, so the simplest method that is good enough should be chosen. For logistic and linear models clinpred uses the closed testing procedure of Vergouwe et al. (2017). Each method is compared with revision (the most flexible) by a likelihood ratio test (F test for linear models), starting from the simplest:





flowchart TD
  A{"Original model<br/>significantly worse than revision?"} -- no --> O["Keep the original model"]
  A -- yes --> B{"Recalibration in the large<br/>significantly worse than revision?"}
  B -- no --> C["Recalibration in the large"]
  B -- yes --> D{"Recalibration<br/>significantly worse than revision?"}
  D -- no --> R["Recalibration"]
  D -- yes --> V["Model revision"]






The procedure protects against updating on noise. The price is power: when revision has many parameters, a one-parameter shift is diluted among them and may not be detected (the external validation example shows a case). Look at the O/E ratio and its confidence interval as well, and decide with clinical judgement.
For Cox models the partial likelihood does not involve the baseline hazard, so a change of the baseline risk cannot be tested against revision the same way. clinpred uses sequential tests from the most complex method down: revision against recalibration (partial likelihood ratio), slope = 1 (partial likelihood ratio), and observed/expected risk at the horizon = 1 (a Wald test of log O/E); the most complex method whose test is significant is chosen.
Updated models are evaluated in the same data that updated them, so their performance is optimistic — most of all for revision. An updated model should itself be validated before use.

title: Clinical prediction models in jamovi
text: A clinical prediction model turns what is known about a patient today (age, sex, blood pressure, a biomarker) into a probability: the risk of having a disease now (diagnostic) or of developing an event later (prognostic). Building one is easy; building one that works in the next patients is not. The model is fitted to the data it is evaluated on, so its apparent performance flatters it; it can be miscalibrated in another hospital or period; and a long list of candidate predictors invites overfitting. This tutorial follows the workflow that the TRIPOD+AI guideline (Collins et al. 2024) and the textbooks (Steyerberg 2019) recommend, and shows each step with the clinpred module for jamovi.

The three development analyses share the same panel and results: predictors (linear, splines, factors, interactions), selection (baseline covariates, stepwise, elastic net), missing data, performance (discrimination, calibration, overall, clinical utility), internal validation (bootstrap, cross-validation), validation in new data (a split of the data or an external file), model updating, sample size, and explanation (effects, importance, SHAP). Every table can carry plain-language notes (Explanations).

title: Clinical prediction models in jamovi
text:
How to read this tutorial

Foundations explains the concepts with as little algebra as possible: what a prediction model is and why it overfits, how its performance is measured, and how it is validated.
Worked examples run the module step by step on one data set. Each page states the question, the options to set in the panel, the tables and plots jamovi shows, and how to read them. Start with the logistic model; the others build on it.
Further maps the module’s output to the TRIPOD+AI reporting items and has a glossary.

Every table and plot in the worked examples is computed by the module’s own code, so it is what jamovi shows with the same options. The folded R syntax under each example is the equivalent call from R (clinpred::cpLogistic(...)), useful for reproducing a result outside jamovi.

title: Clinical prediction models in jamovi
text:
The example data
The examples use a simulated heart cohort of 2400 patients, available in jamovi’s Data Library (☰ → Open → Data Library → Clinical Prediction Models) and here as heart_cohort.omv. It is simulated, so the true model is known: age acts non-linearly, the excess risk of men falls with age (an age × sex interaction), body mass index has some missing values, and the later recruitment period has a slightly lower baseline risk. Each patient has three outcomes:

Predictors: age, sex, smoking (never / former / current), sbp (systolic blood pressure), chol (cholesterol), bmi, diabetes; centre (A, B, C) and period (2012–2016, 2017–2019) describe where and when the patient was recruited.
An external cohort of 1,000 patients from another population, heart_external.csv, is used for external validation. It has the problems real files have: columns named with other capitals, levels spelled differently, unknown categories and values beyond the development range.

title: Clinical prediction models in jamovi
text:
Installing the module
clinpred needs jamovi 28.4 or later (the current series). Download the .jmo file for your computer from the releases page and, in jamovi, choose Modules (⊕) → Sideload. The analyses appear under Prediction. The options, tables and plots are available in English, Spanish and Catalan, following jamovi’s language setting.

title: Validating a published model
text: Question. A paper reports a logistic model for the 10-year cardiovascular risk, as a table of coefficients. Does it work in our patients (the external cohort)? Most published models are never validated outside the data that produced them; this is the analysis that should come before using one.

Shapley decomposition of R²
How much of the model’s explained variation does each predictor contribute? The natural idea — add the predictors one at a time and record how much each raises the R² — has a flaw: the answer depends on the order. title: Missing values
text:
Why it matters
Dropping patients with a missing value (complete-case analysis) loses information and, worse, can bias the model if missingness is related to the outcome. A prediction model also needs a rule for patients with missing values when it is used. Multiple imputation by chained equations is the usual remedy (Steyerberg 2019): each missing value is filled in several times from a model of that variable given all the others including the outcome, the analysis is repeated in each completed data set, and the results are combined.

title: Measuring performance
text:
A prediction model is judged on four aspects (Steyerberg et al. 2010). None of them replaces the others: a model can rank patients well and still give wrong risks, or give right risks that change no decision.
The examples on this page use the logistic model of the heart cohort (age as a spline with an age × sex interaction, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking and diabetes): 2360 patients, 364 of whom had a cardiovascular event within 10 years (15.4%).

title: Measuring performance
text:
Discrimination: the C-statistic
A model discriminates if it gives higher risks to the patients who will have the event than to those who will not. Look at the predicted risks of the two groups:





















Figure 1: Predicted risks of the patients who had an event (orange) and of those who did not (blue). The event group is shifted to the right, but the two overlap a lot.



Patients with an event tend to have higher predicted risks (median 19% against 13%), but the distributions overlap widely: many patients without an event get higher risks than some with one. The C-statistic puts a number on this overlap.

Counting pairs
Take one patient with the event and one without. If the model gave the higher risk to the patient with the event, the pair is concordant; otherwise it is discordant (a tie counts half). The C-statistic is the proportion of concordant pairs among all such pairs. With 4 patients with an event and 5 without there are 4 × 5 = 20 pairs:





















Figure 2: Every pair of one patient with and one without the event. A pair is concordant (✓) when the patient with the event has the higher predicted risk. Here 15 of 20 pairs are concordant: C = 0.75.



Patient A (risk 62%) is ranked above every patient without the event; patient D (9%) above only two of them. 15 of 20 pairs are concordant, so C = 0.75: for a random pair, the model ranks the patient with the event higher 75% of the time. For the heart model the same count over all 364 × 1996 = 726,544 pairs gives C = 0.686.
How to read it: 0.5 is a coin toss (the model ranks no better than chance), 1 is perfect separation. 0.7–0.8 is typical of clinical models built from routine variables; above 0.8 is good. The C-statistic says nothing about whether the risks are right: doubling every risk would not change a single pair.


The ROC curve
For a binary outcome the C-statistic equals the area under the ROC curve (AUC). Choose a threshold — treat everyone above 20% — and count how many patients with the event are above it (sensitivity) and how many without the event are wrongly above it (1 − specificity). Each threshold gives one point; joining all of them, from 100% (nobody above) to 0% (everyone above), draws the ROC curve.





















Figure 3: ROC curve of the heart model. The point marks the 20% threshold; the shaded area under the curve is the C-statistic. The diagonal is a model that ranks at random.



For time-to-event outcomes, Harrell’s C compares the pairs whose order of events is known (the one who had the event first should have the higher risk); Uno’s C weights the pairs for censoring and restricts them to the horizon (Uno et al. 2011); the time-dependent AUC separates the patients with an event by the horizon from those event-free at it. Royston’s D measures the separation of the prognostic index (Royston and Sauerbrei 2004). clinpred gives DeLong’s confidence interval for the AUC (DeLong et al. 1988).
Discrimination depends on the case-mix: in a population where patients differ more, the same model discriminates better. Comparing AUCs across populations needs care (see the external validation example).

title: Measuring performance
text:
Calibration
Calibration is the agreement between predicted risks and observed frequencies: among patients given a 20% risk, about 20% should have the event. It is the aspect most often neglected — “the Achilles heel of predictive analytics” (Van Calster et al. 2019) — and a miscalibrated model misleads every patient it is used on, whatever its AUC.





















Figure 4: Three calibration curves: a well calibrated model lies on the diagonal; an overfitted model has a slope below 1 (low risks too low, high risks too high); a model from a population with a higher incidence predicts too high everywhere.



The measures follow a hierarchy (Van Calster et al. 2019):

Calibration-in-the-large (or the O/E ratio, observed over expected events): is the average risk right? Ideal: 0 (O/E = 1). In the development data it is 0 by construction.
Calibration slope: the slope of the outcome on the model’s linear predictor. Ideal 1; below 1 the predictions are too extreme (typical of overfitting, or of transporting a model to a more homogeneous population); above 1, too modest.
Calibration curve: a smoothed plot of observed against predicted risk (a loess smoother; for Cox models a Cox model on a spline of the predicted risk at the horizon (Austin et al. 2020)), with grouped observed proportions and a histogram of the predictions. Its average absolute distance from the diagonal is the ICI; E50, E90 and Emax are its median, 90th percentile and maximum (Austin and Steyerberg 2019).

text:
Overall performance: the Brier score
The Brier score asks, patient by patient, how far the predicted risk was from what happened. What happened is coded 1 (event) or 0 (no event); the error is the difference, squared so that errors in both directions count, and averaged over patients:
\[\text{Brier} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} (\text{outcome}_i - \text{predicted risk}_i)^2.\]

Lower is better; 0 would be a model that predicts 0% for everyone without the event and 100% for everyone with it.





















Figure 5: The penalty a patient adds to the Brier score, by the risk the model gave: a patient with the event is penalised for a low risk, one without it for a high risk.



The value of a Brier score depends on how common the outcome is, so it needs a reference: a “model” without predictors that gives everyone the average risk (15.4% here) has a Brier score of 15.4% × (1 − 15.4%) = 0.1304. The heart model scores 0.1220. The scaled Brier score is the improvement over that reference: 1 − 0.1220 / 0.1304 = 0.064. The model removes 6.4% of the prediction error of knowing only the average risk — small, as for most models of a long-term outcome built on a few variables, where much of what will happen to an individual is unpredictable. A negative scaled Brier in new patients means the model is worse than the average risk. For Cox models clinpred weights the Brier score for censoring at the horizon (the scaled version is the index of prediction accuracy (Graf et al. 1999; Kattan and Gerds 2018)).
Nagelkerke’s and Cox–Snell’s R² are likelihood-based alternatives; the Cox–Snell R² is the input of the sample size criteria. For a continuous outcome, R² is computed around the mean of the data where it is measured, so it can be negative in validation data; RMSE and MAE are in the units of the outcome.

title: Measuring performance
section: Clinical utility: net benefit and decision curves
text:
Clinical utility: net benefit and decision curves
A good AUC and good calibration do not tell whether using the model helps. Models are used to decide: treat or not, test further or reassure. The question is whether deciding with the model leads to better decisions than the simple alternatives — treat everyone or treat no one.

The threshold is a value judgement
Suppose a statin is offered to patients whose 10-year risk is above 20%. Choosing 20% means: for a patient at exactly 20% risk, treating and not treating are equally good. At that risk, out of 5 such patients 1 will have the event and 4 will not; being indifferent means that the benefit of treating the 1 is judged worth the harm (side effects, cost) of treating the 4. So the threshold fixes an exchange rate between false positives and true positives:

A low threshold suits a cheap, safe intervention; a high one, a risky or expensive one.


Net benefit at one threshold
Net benefit counts the true positives and subtracts the false positives, converted with the exchange rate, per patient (Vickers and Elkin 2006):
\[\text{Net benefit} = \frac{\text{TP}}{N} - \frac{\text{FP}}{N}\times\frac{t}{1-t}.\]
With the heart model at t = 20% (exchange rate 1 : 4), 577 of the 2360 patients are above the threshold: 164 of them had the event (true positives) and 413 did not (false positives). Net benefit = 164/2360 − 413/2360 × 0.25 = 0.0257: as if 2.6 patients per 100 were correctly treated with no one treated unnecessarily.
The alternatives: treat no one has net benefit 0 (no true, no false positives); treat everyone gets all 364 events but also all 1996 non-events: 364/2360 − 1996/2360 × 0.25 = -0.0572, negative — at this threshold, treating everyone does more harm than good. The model beats both, so at 20% deciding with the model is the best of the three strategies.


The decision curve
Different clinicians and patients choose different thresholds, so the calculation is repeated for every threshold:





















Figure 6: Decision curve of the heart model. The shaded band marks the thresholds where deciding with the model gives more net benefit than both treating everyone and treating no one; the point is the 20% threshold worked above.



How to read it: at each threshold on the horizontal axis, the highest line is the best strategy. At very low thresholds (an intervention so safe that you would give it to almost anyone) treat everyone is as good as the model. From about 4% to 41% the model is best: in that range its predictions lead to better decisions. Where the model’s curve falls to the treat no one line, it identifies too few patients above the threshold to matter.
clinpred adds a table at chosen thresholds with the interventions avoided per 100 patients: how many fewer unnecessary treatments than treat everyone, for the same number of true positives — another way of saying the same thing. For Cox models, the risk of the event among the patients above each threshold is estimated by Kaplan–Meier at the horizon, so censoring is accounted for.

title: Measuring performance
text:
What to report
TRIPOD+AI (Collins et al. 2024) asks for discrimination and calibration (with a calibration plot) in the development data corrected for optimism, and in every validation; clinical utility when the model is meant to guide decisions. The reporting page maps each item to clinpred’s output.

title: Prediction models and overfitting
text:
Regression is used for two different purposes. In an aetiological study the question is the effect of one exposure, and the other variables are there to remove confounding: the coefficient of the exposure is the result. In a prediction study no coefficient is the result: the result is the predicted risk of each patient, and the question is whether these risks are accurate (calibration) and separate patients with and without the outcome (discrimination) in patients who were not used to build the model (Steyerberg 2019). A predictor need not be causal; it must only carry information that is available at the moment of prediction.
A diagnostic model predicts the presence of a disease now (e.g. pulmonary embolism in a patient with chest pain); a prognostic model predicts a future event (e.g. a cardiovascular event within 10 years). The tools are the same.

title: Prediction models and overfitting
text:
The steps

Define the outcome and the moment of prediction. Who are the patients, when is the prediction made, and what is predicted by when (a time horizon for prognostic models).
Choose candidate predictors from knowledge, not from the data: what is measured routinely, reliably and before the outcome.
Check the sample size for the number of candidate parameters (below).
Handle missing values (exploration, imputation; see the example).
Specify the model: non-linear effects of continuous predictors (splines), interactions only when expected, no dichotomising of continuous variables.
Estimate it, possibly with selection or penalisation (shrinkage).
Evaluate the performance — discrimination, calibration, overall accuracy and clinical usefulness — and correct it for optimism by internal validation.
Validate it in new patients (another period, centre or population) and, if needed, update it.
Present it so that others can use it (the full equation, a calculator) and report it following TRIPOD+AI (Collins et al. 2024).

clinpred covers steps 3 to 9.

title: Prediction models and overfitting
text:
Overfitting and optimism
A model fitted to a data set describes that data set best, noise included. Its apparent performance, measured in the same patients, is therefore optimistic: in new patients the discrimination will be lower and the predictions too extreme (high risks too high, low risks too low). The more parameters relative to the number of events, the larger the optimism.
The simulation below shows it. Each data set has 300 patients (about 45 events) and three real predictors; noise predictors are then added. The apparent C-statistic (AUC) keeps rising with every useless predictor, while the AUC in a large independent sample falls. The bootstrap optimism-corrected AUC, computed by clinpred’s own validation engine, removes most of the optimism. It removes less of it when the parameters approach the number of events: there the data are too few even to estimate the optimism, which is one more reason to respect the sample size (below).





















Figure 1: Apparent, bootstrap-corrected and true (new-patient) AUC of logistic models with 3 real predictors and an increasing number of noise predictors; 300 patients, means of 12 simulated data sets.



With 30 noise predictors (33 parameters for about 45 events) the apparent AUC is 0.864, but in new patients it is 0.664; the bootstrap says 0.746. The bootstrap also estimates how much the predictions are too extreme: the calibration slope of the model in new patients, 0.43 here (1 would be perfect). This is the uniform shrinkage factor: multiplying the coefficients by it would make the predictions about right. The validation page explains how the bootstrap does this.
The remedies are, in order: fewer candidate parameters (pre-specification from knowledge), more data, and penalised estimation (shrinkage, elastic net). Selection by p-values or AIC does not remove the optimism — it adds its own — unless it is repeated inside the validation, as clinpred does.

title: Prediction models and overfitting
Glossary
text:
Apparent performance. Performance measured in the data used to develop the model; optimistic.
Baseline covariates. Predictors forced into the model and never selected or penalised (in clinpred also the baseline model of the incremental-value analysis).
Bootstrap. Resampling the patients with replacement to imitate drawing new samples from the population; used to estimate optimism, shrinkage and stability.
Brier score. Mean squared difference between predicted risk and outcome; scaled Brier compares it with a model without predictors.
Calibration. Agreement between predicted risks and observed frequencies. In the large: the average; slope: the spread; curve: across the range.
Case-mix. The distribution of patient characteristics in a population; it affects discrimination and calibration.
C-statistic (AUC). Probability that a patient with the event has a higher predicted risk than one without; 0.5 is chance.
Closed testing procedure. A sequence of tests choosing the simplest updating method that is not significantly worse than revising the whole model.
Cross-validation. Splitting the data into k folds, predicting each with a model fitted on the others.
Decision curve. Net benefit of a model across risk thresholds, compared with treating all and treating none.
Elastic net. Penalised regression mixing the lasso (sets coefficients to 0) and ridge (shrinks them); λ is the strength of the penalty.
External validation. Evaluating the model, unchanged, in patients from another time, place or setting.
Horizon. The time by which a time-to-event model predicts the risk.
ICI. Integrated calibration index: mean absolute distance between the smoothed calibration curve and the diagonal.
Incremental value. What added predictors contribute over a baseline model.
Linear predictor (prognostic index). The weighted sum of the predictors, before the transformation into a risk.
Membership c-statistic. How well a model separates development from validation patients: a summary of how different the populations are.
Multiple imputation. Filling in missing values several times from models of each variable, analysing each completed data set and pooling the results.
Net benefit. True positives minus false positives weighted by the threshold odds, per patient.
O/E ratio. Observed over expected (predicted) number of events.
Optimism. The difference between apparent and true performance in new patients.
Overfitting. Fitting the noise of the development data; predictions too extreme in new patients.
SHAP value. A predictor’s contribution to one patient’s prediction relative to the average patient.
Shapley decomposition. Sharing the model’s R² among predictors by averaging their gains over all orders of entry.
Shrinkage factor. The factor by which coefficients should be multiplied to correct for overfitting (the expected calibration slope).
Spline (restricted cubic). A smooth, flexible curve for a continuous predictor, linear beyond the outer knots.
Updating. Adapting a model to a new population: recalibration in the large, recalibration, or revision.
